newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Colombian mountain DJ pleads for peace.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Colombian mountain DJ pleads for peace.

text.p: When this mountain village in Colombia's Cauca province came under guerrilla attack for the first time in several years, Jose Domingo Garcia knew exactly what to do: The 40-year-old farmer sprang out of bed, set up his tape deck and microphones and started recording the sounds of war.

"I play the tape as a reminder," Domingo said, standing on the porch of his four-room farmhouse a couple of miles (km) of winding mud road above Siberia in this lush but steep river valley about 215 miles (350 km) southwest of Bogota.

Domingo is the owner and sole disc jockey for Siberia Verde Stereo, a 20-kilowatt radio station he built three years ago to call for an end to slash-and-burn agriculture while spinning the latest salsa and "vallenato" hits. But his radio commentary has turned from environmental awareness to pleas for peace as three major towns in the 18-mile (25 km) range of his broadcasts -- Siberia, Caldono and Silvia -- have been hit at least once by leftist insurgents in recent months.

His tape of the attack on Siberia now provides a frequent background to his commentaries and appeals for an end to Latin America's longest-running guerrilla conflict. "I started broadcasting because I noticed that each year there was less water in the rivers," he said. "But I want people to know that the war can poison the environment too."
NO MORE PEACE FOR SIBERIA, NEIGHBOURS
Colombia has seen more than three decades of armed conflict. But while Siberia, Caldono and Silvia lie in areas of strong guerrilla presence, they had remained relatively free from violence.

Then, in February, Colombia's largest rebel group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), twice rained rocket-propelled grenades on police installations in Caldono. FARC rebels attacked Siberia the same day, wounding six policemen. And a 17-year-old student was killed last month when the FARC assaulted the jail and agrarian savings bank in Silvia, whose weekly market had become a tourist destination.

The narrow streets of Siberia and Caldono are now filled with young soldiers lounging on the painted stoops or peering over walls pockmarked by gunfire. "It's taken a while for the people to get used to having the military here," Caldono's Mayor Dodamin Trujillo Noguera said "It makes them nervous."
Radio Verde, often overwhelmed by larger stations or distorted by the weather, has helped keep residents of this remote mountain valley connected, Trujillo said.
Domingo makes local announcements, provides an on-the-air lost-and-found service and raises funds for causes such as refurbishing a local school.

When he senses an oppressive mood among farmers, he reads passages from a dog-eared copy of a Deepak Chopra positive-thinking manual -- that is, until the mountain humdity affects his transmitter and he must shut down for a few minutes while he readjusts the system.
"Sometimes we get Radio National Cauca better," valley farmer Jorge Trujillo said."But we'd rather listen to Jose Domingo."

Like most of the peasant farmers in the region, Domingo rises at dawn to tend to the coffee, beans and corn he grows on the steep mountain slopes surrounding his home. But by midday he is at the microphone behind a wooden console he has covered with letters and mementoes sent by his listeners.
In one corner he keeps a plastic cup filled with the spent assault rifle cartridges he has found while walking the fields.
"Search for peace in Colombia," Domingo announces over the air in the bass tones of a radio dee-jay, his recording of the rebel attack on Siberia fading into the upbeat rhythm of a salsa tune.
